- Once you start ordering investigations, do not go back to broad history taking unless absolutely required to clarify a specific test result.

- Do not finalize the case based on history or physical examination alone if additional available investigations would materially affect the diagnosis.

The preserved bulbocavernosus reflex with absent perianal sensation and a dense paraplegia indicates a true cord (myelopathic) lesion rather than a conus/cauda equina or peripheral neuropathic process; the pain-first-then-progressive-deficit sequence is characteristic of an expanding space-occupying lesion in the spinal canal.

Differential considered: acute transverse myelitis (including AQP4/MOG-associated and MS-related disease), spinal epidural abscess, spontaneous epidural haematoma, compressive thoracic disc or tumour/metastasis, spinal cord infarction (including aortic pathology), and spinal dural arteriovenous fistula. There was no fever, no infection source, no injection drug use and no constitutional or oncological history; no visual symptoms or prior relapses to suggest a demyelinating disease; and the deficit evolved over two days rather than the hyperacute minutes-to-hours onset typical of cord infarction.

Investigations: Urgent whole-spine MRI with and without contrast was the decisive test and demonstrated an epidural haematoma compressing the cord and posterior thecal sac from C6 to T2, with no traumatic or underlying structural lesion identified. Blood tests showed a normal platelet count (250,000/µL), PT 12 s with INR 1.0 and aPTT 30 s, excluding an underlying coagulopathy or anticoagulant effect as the cause; the mild neutrophilic leucocytosis (WBC 13,000/µL, 85% neutrophils) is consistent with an acute stress response to cord compression. CRP, ESR, metabolic panel, LDH, ANA, AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG, B12, HIV and syphilis serology, blood cultures and TB IGRA were not available in this case, but none were required once the MRI established a compressive haematoma and the clinical picture showed no features of infection, demyelination or metabolic myelopathy.

Conclusion: The combination of a compressive cervicothoracic epidural blood collection on MRI, normal coagulation and platelets, absence of trauma or anticoagulation, and absence of infective features establishes spontaneous spinal epidural haematoma with acute compressive myelopathy. Management is immediate neurosurgical decompression (laminectomy and evacuation of the haematoma), with urinary catheterisation, bowel care, pressure-area and VTE prophylaxis, and intensive rehabilitation; neurological recovery is time-dependent, and no further diagnostic testing should delay surgery.
